titre: The Venus de Milo: The Base That Dated It, and Disappeared
accroche: In 1820, an inscribed base came with the statue found on Milos. It tied her to the Hellenistic era, not the classical age hoped for. It disappeared.
contenu_vulgarise:
On April 8, 1820, on the Greek island of Milos, a farmer digging unearths a marble statue in several pieces. A French naval officer, Olivier Voutier, witnesses the scene and encourages him to keep going. Along with the two large pieces of the statue and a third, smaller one, a fragment of an arm, a hand holding an apple and two herms, pillars topped with a head, are found. The statue has no arms; scientific analyses carried out during her 2010 restoration support the view that the hand holding the apple belongs to the statue. After negotiations with the local authorities, the statue is bought for 1,000 francs and reaches Paris in February 1821; the Marquis de Rivière, France's ambassador to the Ottomans, offers it to Louis XVIII, who gives it to the Louvre.

## A Base That Would Have Changed Everything

In a third lot of marble sent along with the statue is a base bearing an inscription. One side of it is broken; according to Gregory Curtis's account, when it is pushed against the statue's left side, the two pieces fit perfectly. The inscription, restored as "[...]andros, son of Menides, of Antioch on the Maeander," names a sculptor from a city founded after 280 BCE. It would therefore place the work in the Hellenistic period, not in the classical age of Phidias and Praxiteles, to which the French consul in Athens had assigned it. A drawing attributed to Auguste Debay shows this base fitted into the statue's plinth.

## A Louvre Hoping for Something Else

France emerges from Waterloo stripped of its trophies: the Treaty of Vienna demanded the return of some 5,000 works seized by Napoleon's troops, and the Apollo Belvedere went back to the Vatican in 1815. The Count de Forbin, director of the Louvre, wants a Greek masterpiece of the classical age. He and his scholars judge that the base is the product of a late, crude restoration that has nothing to do with the statue. Scholars who argue the opposite, such as the Count de Clarac, are barred from the workshop. In April 1821, Forbin gets Quatremère de Quincy to write a paper for the Académie des Beaux-Arts tying the statue to the school of Praxiteles. This official French position lasts more than a hundred and thirty years. The inscribed base, for its part, is no longer at the Louvre: Alain Pasquier, the museum's general curator of Greek antiquities, has spent hours searching for it in the storerooms, without success.

## A Date Recovered by Another Route

The base's disappearance makes it impossible either to prove or to rule out that it belonged to the statue. Rachel Kousser and Jean-Luc Martinez doubt the link: Debay's drawing does not show the missing left foot, which would have rested on it, and in a sketch by Voutier the plaque serves as the base of one of the herms. But the later dating ended up prevailing without it: in 1893, the German archaeologist Adolf Furtwängler places the work between 150 and 50 BCE, "contrary to general opinion," as a Louvre curator put it in 1951, when the nineteenth-century consensus leaned toward the fourth century BCE. This dating is now widely accepted, and Pasquier does not dispute it. The Venus de Milo, one of the most famous Greek statues in the world, is therefore not from the classical age she was long assumed to belong to. And the piece that could have revealed it as early as 1820 has vanished, with no way of knowing whether it was because it was inconvenient, or simply because it got lost.

repere.texte: An inscribed base, found with the statue in 1820 and later lost, named a sculptor from Antioch on the Maeander, a city founded after 280 BCE, which would place the work in the Hellenistic period. Furtwängler proposed this dating in 1893 (150 to 50 BCE), and it is now widely accepted.
repere.source: Smithsonian Magazine, "Base Deception," Gregory Curtis, 2003; Wikipedia, "Venus de Milo"

quiz.question: What does the disappearance of the inscribed base found with the Venus de Milo in 1820 change about its history?
choix: It prevents us from knowing whether the statue depicts Aphrodite or another goddess
It prevents us from proving that this base belonged to the statue, and so from relying on it to date her
It proves that the entire statue is a fake made in the twentieth century
It prevents us from knowing whether the arms were lost before or after the discovery
quiz.explication: The lost base can neither prove nor rule out that it belonged to the statue, since it no longer exists to be examined. The Hellenistic dating widely accepted today was put forward by Furtwängler in 1893, against the general opinion of the time.
